The Optimizer's Curse

An interactive companion to marimo's video "The Optimizer's Curse".
You win an auction. You feel great. Then someone tells you 100 people were bidding. Suddenly you feel a lot worse.
Whenever you pick the maximum of noisy estimates, the winner is, on average, the most over-optimistic estimate. In auctions that is the winner's curse; in machine learning (hyperparameter search, model selection, evals) it is the optimizer's curse. This notebook replays the video's simulations so you can feel why it happens and how to guard against it.

data.text/markdown: Pick an answer above; section 1 will tell you who's right.

1 · The winner's curse

Everyone at the auction forms a value belief: the true value ||(v||) plus some estimation noise, ||[b_i = v + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2), \qquad i = 1,\dots,N.||]Nobody is biased: each single estimate is right on average. But the auctioneer doesn't take an average, he takes the maximum: ||[\text{winning bid} = \max_i b_i, \qquad E[\max_i b_i] = v + \sigma\, e_N, \qquad e_N = E[\max \text{ of } N \text{ standard normals}] > 0.||]||(e_N||) grows with ||(N||) (≈1.87 for 20 bidders, ≈2.51 for 100, ≈3.24 for 1000). The more people bid, the more the winner overpays. Press ▶ play: each frame is one auction. The dots are the ||(N||) bids, the red one wins, and the histogram below collects winning bids.

data.text/markdown:
2 · The remedy: shade your bid

The video's notebook has sliders for the actual value, the bidders' belief μ, σ, and the number of candidates N. If (big if) you can quantify your own doubt ||(\hat\sigma||) and guess how many people are bidding, the theory hands you the expected overpayment, so you can subtract it up front: ||[\text{shaded bid} = b - \hat\sigma \, e_N .||]It is a function from number of candidates → overpayment, which you then invert to bring the overpayment back to zero. You'll be more conservative and lose some auctions, but the auctions you win will no longer be at a loss on average.

data.text/markdown:
3 · The optimizer's curse: a dice game

Player A and player B each roll a d20 to see who is "better at rolling". Over many rounds they're equally good. Then B starts to cheat: he rolls k dice and only reports the maximum. The maximum of ||(k||) d20 rolls has ||[P(M \le m) = \left(\tfrac{m}{20}\right)^k \quad\Rightarrow\quad P(M = m) = \left(\tfrac{m}{20}\right)^k - \left(\tfrac{m-1}{20}\right)^k .||]For ||(k=1||) the distribution is flat; for ||(k=2||) it's a staircase that walks up to 20; for ||(k=100||) it's "practically impossible not to roll a 20". Nothing about B's dice changed. Only the reporting rule did.

4 · Is this machine learning? Yes: hyperparameter search

A randomized search tries n_iter settings and reports the best cross-validation score. Every CV score is "true quality + noise" (which folds, which random seed, which shuffle). Picking the max is exactly player B rolling more dice: ||[\text{reported score} = \max_{j \le n_\text{iter}} \big(q_j + \varepsilon_j\big) \quad\text{tends to exceed}\quad q_{j^*} .||]So with more iterations you may not be optimizing the model; you may be optimizing the random number generator. First a pure version: imagine every configuration is equally good (true accuracy 0.80) and CV adds a bit of noise.

data.text/markdown:
5 · Sandbox: options that really differ, and a Bayesian remedy

So far everyone was equally good. In real life the options do differ: true values ||(q_j \sim \mathcal N(\mu_0, \tau^2)||), and we see noisy estimates ||(x_j = q_j + \varepsilon_j||), ||(\varepsilon_j \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_j^2)||). We pick the largest estimate and expect to get ||(x_{j^*}||). Smith & Winkler (2006), who named the optimizer's curse, show the fix is to shrink every estimate toward the prior before choosing: ||[\hat q_j = \mu_0 + \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma_j^2}\,(x_j - \mu_0).||]Noisier estimates get shrunk harder, so with unequal noise, shrinkage can even change which option you pick. Each dot is one option in one simulated decision; red = the naive pick, blue = the shrunk pick.

Idea What happens Formula / rule Remedy
Winner's curse The highest of N unbiased bids is biased upward ||(E[\max b_i] = v + \sigma e_N||) Shade: bid ||(b - \hat\sigma e_N||)

Shrinkage Noisy estimates pulled toward the prior ||(\hat q = \mu_0 + \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}(x-\mu_0)||) Removes expected disappointment, picks better options
One sentence: whenever you select the maximum of noisy numbers, expect to be disappointed, by about noise × e_N.
